items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have a random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
We've already seen that the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X},] given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X}
= \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

Content:
is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \mu,] which means that

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu.]

Content:
The definition of the sample mean follows naturally from the definition of [MATH: \mu.]

Content:
However, when constructing estimators for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] things are not so simple!

Content:
From the definition of the population variance, you might expect that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2]

Content:
is an unbiased estimator for [MATH: \sigma^2.] However, it can be shown that it is a biased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2,] meaning that

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[\dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2\right] \neq \sigma^2.]

Content:
This might seem surprising, but it's true.

Content:
To compute an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2,] we use the so-called sample variance. The sample variance is denoted [MATH: S^2,] and is defined as

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.]

Content:
At the end of this lesson, we will prove that [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2].

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Notice that instead of dividing by [MATH: n] (as with our original biased estimator), we instead divide by [MATH: n-1.] This is sometimes referred to as Bessel's correction, as it corrects the bias of the original estimator.
- We should think of [MATH: S^2] as a random variable whose value varies according to the particular sample under consideration.
- Since [MATH: S^2] is a random variable, it has a sampling distribution (i.e., a probability distribution). We'll learn more about the sampling distribution of [MATH: S^2] in future lessons.

Content:
Finally, we have an alternative formula for the sample variance that's often more convenient in practice:

Content:
[MATH: S^2 =\dfrac{n}{n-1}\left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right]]

Content:
We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

items.title: Computing an Estimate of the Population Variance

sections.normalized_html:
A random sample of size [MATH: n=81] is conducted from a population. It is known that

[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{81} \left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2 = 180]

where each [MATH: x_i] is a sample observation. Compute an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation.
sections.readable_text:
A random sample of size [MATH: n=81] is conducted from a population. It is known that

[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{81} \left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2 = 180]

where each [MATH: x_i] is a sample observation. Compute an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation.
EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is given by

[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right] .]

Note that

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] and

  • [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = s^2] denotes an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2] that's computed from the sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

We're given that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{81} \left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2 = 180] and [MATH: n=81.] Therefore,

[MATH: σ^(^)^{2}|= s^{2}; = (1)/(n − 1)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))^{2}; = (1)/(81 − 1) ⋅ 180; = (1)/(80) ⋅ 180; = 2.25.]

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = 2.25.] We take the square root to compute an unbiased estimate of the standard deviation. This gives

[MATH: \hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{2.25} = 1.5.]

sections.normalized_html:

Compute an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

[MATH: \overline{x^2} - \left( \overline{x} \right)^2 = 4.]

Compute an unbiased estimate of the population variance.
EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is given by

[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right] .]

Note that

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] and

  • [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = s^2] denotes an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2] that's computed from the sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

Here, there are [MATH: n=9] data points in the sample, and we have

[MATH: \overline{x^2} - \left( \overline{x} \right)^2 = 4.]

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is

[MATH: σ^(^)^{2}|= s^{2}; = (n)/(n − 1)[x^{2}^(―) − (x^(―))^{2}]; = (9)/(9 − 1) ⋅ 4; = (36)/(8); = 4.5.]

[MATH: 5, \quad 3, \quad 6, \quad 4, \quad 7]

Suppose the following data is sampled from a population. Compute an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

[MATH: 5, \quad 3, \quad 6, \quad 4, \quad 7]
EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is given by

[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right] .]

Note that

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] and

  • [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = s^2] denotes the unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2] computed from the sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

First, we will compute the quantity

[MATH: \overline{x^2} - \left( \overline{x} \right)^2.]

We proceed as follows:

  • The mean of the data is given by [MATH: x^(―)|= (1)/(5)(5 + 3 + 6 + 4 + 7); = (25)/(5); = 5.]

  • The mean of the squared data is given by [MATH: x^{2}^(―)|= (1)/(5)(5^{2} + 3^{2} + 6^{2} + 4^{2} + 7^{2}); = (135)/(5); = 27.]

Therefore,

[MATH: x^{2}^(―) − (x^(―))^{2}|= 27 − 5^{2}; = 2.]

Finally, the sample variance is

[MATH: σ^(^)^{2}|= s^{2}; = (n)/(n − 1)[x^{2}^(―) − (x^(―))^{2}]; = (5)/(5 − 1) ⋅ 2; = 2.5.]

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is [MATH: 2.5.]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[S^2\right] = \sigma^2.]

Content:
A major step towards this goal is to find the expected value of the sum of squares term:
[MATH: \textrm E \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 \right] \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
First, consider the following sum of squares:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n \left((X_i - \overline X) + (\overline X - \mu)\right)^2]

where we have used the fact that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \overline X) = 0] and that [MATH: (\overline X - \mu)] does not depend on [MATH: i]. Thus, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 + n(\overline X- \mu)^2.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 - n(\overline X- \mu)^2 . \qquad\qquad (\ast\ast)]

Content:
Notice that the left-hand side is the summation term [MATH: (\ast)] we wish to find the expectation of.

Content:

Content:
[MATH: E[(X_{i} − μ)^{2}]|= σ^{2}; E[(X^(―) − μ)^{2}]|= Var[X^(―)] = (σ^{2})/(n)]

[MATH: \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
We've already seen that the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X},] given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X}
= \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

Content:
is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \mu,] which means that

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu.]

Content:
The definition of the sample mean follows naturally from the definition of [MATH: \mu.]

Content:
However, when constructing estimators for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] things are not so simple!

Content:
From the definition of the population variance, you might expect that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2]

Content:
is an unbiased estimator for [MATH: \sigma^2.] However, it can be shown that it is a biased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2,] meaning that

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[\dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2\right] \neq \sigma^2.]

Content:
This might seem surprising, but it's true.

Content:
To compute an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2,] we use the so-called sample variance. The sample variance is denoted [MATH: S^2,] and is defined as

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.]

Content:
At the end of this lesson, we will prove that [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2].

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Notice that instead of dividing by [MATH: n] (as with our original biased estimator), we instead divide by [MATH: n-1.] This is sometimes referred to as Bessel's correction, as it corrects the bias of the original estimator.
- We should think of [MATH: S^2] as a random variable whose value varies according to the particular sample under consideration.
- Since [MATH: S^2] is a random variable, it has a sampling distribution (i.e., a probability distribution). We'll learn more about the sampling distribution of [MATH: S^2] in future lessons.

Content:
Finally, we have an alternative formula for the sample variance that's often more convenient in practice:

Content:
[MATH: S^2 =\dfrac{n}{n-1}\left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right]]

Content:
We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing an Estimate of the Population Variance

Example Prompt:
A random sample of size [MATH: n=81] is conducted from a population. It is known that

[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^{81} \left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2 = 180]

where each [MATH: x_i] is a sample observation. Compute an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n] is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from a population with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is given by

[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{n-1} \left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right] .]

Note that

- [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,
- the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] and
- [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = s^2] denotes an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2] that's computed from the sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

We're given that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{81} \left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2 = 180] and [MATH: n=81.] Therefore,

[MATH: σ^(^)^{2}|= s^{2}; = (1)/(n − 1)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))^{2}; = (1)/(81 − 1) ⋅ 180; = (1)/(80) ⋅ 180; = 2.25.]

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = 2.25.] We take the square root to compute an unbiased estimate of the standard deviation. This gives

[MATH: \hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{2.25} = 1.5.]

- [MATH: \hat{\sigma}^2 = s^2] denotes an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2] that's computed from the sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

[MATH: x^{2}^(―) − (x^(―))^{2}|= 27 − 5^{2}; = 2.]

Finally, the sample variance is

[MATH: σ^(^)^{2}|= s^{2}; = (n)/(n − 1)[x^{2}^(―) − (x^(―))^{2}]; = (5)/(5 − 1) ⋅ 2; = 2.5.]

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is [MATH: 2.5.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Proof of the Alternative Formula

Content:
Here, we will show that

Content:
[MATH: S^2 =\dfrac{n}{n-1}\left[ \overline{X^2} - \left( \overline{X} \right)^2 \right].]

Content:
We start with the definition of [MATH: S^2\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2]

Content:
Expanding the parentheses and distributing the summation, we have

Content:
[MATH: S^{2}|= (1)/(n − 1)∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{2} − 2X_{i}X^(―) + (X^(―))^{2}; = (1)/(n − 1)[∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{2} − ∑_(i = 1)^(n)2X_{i}X^(―) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X^(―))^{2}]; = (1)/(n − 1)[∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{2} − 2X^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i} + (X^(―))^{2} ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(n)1].]

Content:
We now consider each sum separately:

Content:
- [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 = n\cdot \overline{X^2}] follows directly from the definition of the mean of [MATH: X^2]
- [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = n\cdot \overline{X}] follows directly from the definition of the mean of [MATH: X]
- [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n 1 = \underbrace{1+1+\cdots+1}_{n\, \textrm{times}} = n]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: S^{2}|= (1)/(n − 1)[∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i}^{2} − 2X^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)X_{i} + (X^(―))^{2} ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(n)1]; = (1)/(n − 1)[n ⋅ X^{2}^(―) − 2X^(―) ⋅ n ⋅ X^(―) + (X^(―))^{2} ⋅ n]; = (n)/(n − 1)[X^{2}^(―) − 2(X^(―))^{2} + (X^(―))^{2}]; = (n)/(n − 1)[X^{2}^(―) − (X^(―))^{2}],]

as required.

Item 12 — Tutorial: Proof That the Sample Variance Is an Unbiased Estimator

Content:
Recall that for a sample of size [MATH: n,] the sample variance [MATH: S^2] is given by

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2.]

Content:
We will now prove that [MATH: S^2] is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2,] that is,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}\left[S^2\right] = \sigma^2.]

Content:
A major step towards this goal is to find the expected value of the sum of squares term:
[MATH: \textrm E \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 \right] \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
First, consider the following sum of squares:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2]

Content:
We can rewrite this term by adding and subtracting the sample mean [MATH: \overline X,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n \left((X_i - \overline X) + (\overline X - \mu)\right)^2]
Squaring and applying the laws of summations, we get

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(n)((X_{i} − X^(―)) + (X^(―) − μ))^{2}|=; ∑_(i = 1)^(n)((X_{i} − X^(―))^{2} + 2(X_{i} − X^(―))(X^(―) − μ) + (X^(―) − μ)^{2})|=; ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2} + 2∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))(X^(―) − μ) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X^(―) − μ)^{2}|=; ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2} + 2(X^(―) − μ)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―)) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X^(―) − μ)^{2}|=; ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2} + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X^(―) − μ)^{2}|=; ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2} + n(X^(―) − μ)^{2}]
where we have used the fact that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \overline X) = 0] and that [MATH: (\overline X - \mu)] does not depend on [MATH: i]. Thus, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 + n(\overline X- \mu)^2.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 - n(\overline X- \mu)^2 . \qquad\qquad (\ast\ast)]

Content:
Notice that the left-hand side is the summation term [MATH: (\ast)] we wish to find the expectation of.

Content:
Now, we make use of the following results:

Content:
[MATH: E[(X_{i} − μ)^{2}]|= σ^{2}; E[(X^(―) − μ)^{2}]|= Var[X^(―)] = (σ^{2})/(n)]

Content:
Finding the expectation of [MATH: (\ast\ast),] we have

Content:
[MATH: E[∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2}]|= E[∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − μ)^{2}] − nE[(X^(―) − μ)^{2}]; = nσ^{2} − n ⋅ (σ^{2})/(n); = nσ^{2} − σ^{2}; = (n − 1)σ^{2}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: E[(1)/(n)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2}] = ((n − 1)σ^{2})/(n).]

Content:
This tells us that the statistic

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2]

Content:
is a biased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2.] Therefore, to form an unbiased estimate of [MATH: \sigma^2,] we must divide our summation term by [MATH: n-1,] not [MATH: n.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: E[S^{2}]|= E[(1)/(n − 1)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(X_{i} − X^(―))^{2}]; = (1)/(n − 1) ⋅ (n − 1)σ^{2}; = σ^{2}]

Content:
as required.
